analysis.one_liner: Reinstates expired taxes on polluting companies to fund toxic waste site cleanups through 2020.
analysis.headline: Ten Democratic senators backed the bill, but it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: From 1980 to 1995, companies that handled hazardous chemicals paid a dedicated tax into the Superfund, the program that cleans up the nation's worst toxic waste sites. Those taxes expired at the end of 1995, and cleanup costs have been paid by ordinary taxpayers ever since. This bill would have brought the polluter taxes back — a tax on petroleum and chemical feedstocks plus a small corporate environmental income tax — through the end of 2020 to refill the fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and people living near toxic waste sites. The tax burden for cleaning up hazardous waste would shift back onto the companies that produced or handled the chemicals, and the Superfund would get a dedicated revenue stream instead of competing for general taxpayer dollars.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near toxic sites

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate (an excise tax on petroleum and hazardous chemical feedstocks) and the corporate environmental income tax, both of which lapsed at the end of 1995, through December 31, 2020 [S2] [S3].
The bill's stated purpose is to extend financing of the Superfund, shifting cleanup funding from general revenues back to a dedicated polluter-funded account [S3].

With the taxes gone, Superfund cleanup has been paid out of general taxpayer funds, meaning the public has been covering costs generated by hazardous-substance producers since 1996 — a shift this bill would reverse [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that refine or import petroleum and manufacture or import hazardous chemicals, plus large corporations generally through the corporate environmental income tax. Some of the cost could be passed along in product prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Petroleum and chemical companies, large corporations

drawbacks.text: Excise taxes on petroleum and chemical inputs do not trace to any individual polluter — the bill's revenues would come from companies by volume of chemicals handled, not necessarily from those responsible for the mess at any specific site [S3].

Reinstating industry taxes on petrochemical feedstocks would likely raise some costs for fuel and chemical products, though the rates are modest and were in place for fifteen years without elimination of the industries affected [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill restores a funding arrangement that existed for fifteen years: dedicated taxes on hazardous-substance handlers paying for hazardous-waste cleanup, instead of general taxpayers footing the bill. The costs are modest taxes on a specific industry; the benefit is cleanup money for toxic sites that threaten public health. The main honest objection is that the tax keys off volume of chemicals handled rather than culpability at any given site — an imperfect match — but the alternative status quo leaves everyone's taxes covering industry-linked cleanup.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on March 2, 2011 by Sen. Lautenberg with eight original co-sponsors, all Democrats [S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on the same day [S5] [S1].
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 112th Congress expired on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Petroleum, petrochemical, and other large corporate taxpayers continued paying nothing into the Superfund, leaving ordinary taxpayers to cover hazardous-waste cleanup costs from general revenues.

sides.party_line_note: All nine cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached the floor, so no voting record exists.

industries.note: Would have paid the reinstated Superfund excise tax on petroleum and hazardous chemical feedstocks. Since the tax lapsed in 1995, the cleanup costs these industries' materials generated have been shifted to general taxpayers.
Would have paid the reinstated corporate environmental income tax through 2020, a small levy tied to corporate income that expired with the Superfund taxes in 1995.
Would stop indirectly subsidizing hazardous-waste cleanup out of general revenues, as has been the case since the Superfund taxes expired.
